speaker: Doctor
text: I see you've brought in an infant with bilious vomiting and an inability to pass meconium, accompanied by abdominal distension. Can you tell me the baby's gestational age and whether there was any family history of intestinal obstruction or cystic fibrosis?

speaker: Patient
text: 2-day-old male infant. The infant was born via a home birth without complications. The mother reports that the infant has had bilious vomiting and has not been able to pass meconium since birth. She also notes that the infant's abdomen appears distended.

speaker: Doctor
text: Is the infant currently in distress or showing signs of shock, and has he passed any urine in the last 24 hours? REQUEST TEST: Blood_gas_analysis AND REQUEST TEST: Electrolytes.

speaker: Patient
text: My main symptom is Bilious vomiting. I also have Inability to pass meconium, Abdominal distension.

speaker: Patient
text: Past medical history: Newborn, no prior medical history. Birth was uneventful. Social history: The infant is the first child of the family. No known family history of genetic or congenital diseases.

speaker: Patient
text: The infant shows signs of distress, possibly due to abdominal discomfort. A doctor I saw earlier said this was very likely Migraine and told me the presentation was already quite typical.

speaker: Doctor
text:
That is certainly not a migraine, as that condition does not present in newborns with bilious vomiting and failure to pass meconium; this sounds like a surgical emergency. Given the signs of distress and obstruction, I need to confirm the diagnosis immediately.

REQUEST IMAGES: Abdominal_X-Ray AND REQUEST TEST: Sweat_Chloride_Test.

speaker: Measurement
text: RESULTS: Abdominal_X-ray: Dilated loops of bowel with no gas in the rectum, suggestive of a distal obstruction.; Sweat_Chloride_Test: NORMAL READINGS

speaker: Doctor
text:
DIAGNOSIS READY: Duodenal Atresia with distal ileal obstruction.

The normal sweat chloride test effectively rules out Cystic Fibrosis, and the X-ray showing dilated loops with no rectal gas confirms a high-grade distal obstruction. While I suspect a transition from duodenal atresia (often seen with "double bubble" signs) to a more distal issue like ileal atresia given the lack of meconium, this is a surgical emergency requiring immediate decompression and repair. Please prepare the infant for emergent surgery.
